Alright, I've just finished a long series of file edits and creations. The user (or the higher-level plan) wanted the project to be functional, and I've been systematically fixing bugs, adding missing modules, and updating UI strings. Now that the core files are in place—`battle.js`, `input.js`, `overworld.js`, `ui.js`, `game.js`, and the HTML index—it's time to verify that the JavaScript syntax across the whole `js` directory is valid. If there are any syntax errors, the game will fail to run, and I want to catch those early before moving on to runtime testing or further feature work.

I could manually open each file and run a linter, but that would be tedious and error‑prone. The environment provides a PowerShell tool that can execute shell commands, and I can leverage Node's built‑in `--check` flag to perform a quick syntax validation without executing the code. The pattern `node --check <file>` returns a non‑zero exit code if the file contains syntax errors, and otherwise exits silently. To make the output more informative, I can pipe each result through a `Write-Output` that prefixes successful checks with "OK <filename>", so I get a clear list of which files passed.

I need to target all JavaScript files in the `js` folder of the project. Using `Get-ChildItem D:\project-5\js\*.js` will enumerate them. Then `ForEach-Object { node --check $_.FullName && Write-Output "OK $($_.Name)" }` will run the check on each file and print the OK line only when the check succeeds (because `&&` only runs the second command on success). This will give me a concise report: any file that fails will produce no "OK" line, and the PowerShell command will surface the error output from Node, which I can review.

Thus, the next logical step is to invoke the PowerShell tool with exactly this command, providing a description that clarifies the intent: "Syntax-check all game JS files". This will let me confirm that all the edits I've made haven't introduced any syntax problems before I respond to the user.

Now I will issue the PowerShell tool call with the constructed command and description.
